qs.q: A patient is evaluated for chronic endogenous hypercortisolism caused by a pituitary adenoma. What finding is expected regarding plasma ACTH and adrenal appearance?
o: Suppressed ACTH with a unilateral benign nodule
High ACTH with bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
Suppressed ACTH with bilateral adrenal atrophy
Very high ACTH with a single necrotic mass
qs.e: Cushing's disease (pituitary adenoma) results in high ACTH production, which drives bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Exogenous steroid use leads to suppressed ACTH and bilateral atrophy.

qs.q: Which pituitary adenoma type is the most common functioning pituitary tumor?
qs.e: Lactotroph adenomas secrete prolactin and represent the most common type of functioning pituitary adenoma. Somatotroph adenomas are less common and secrete growth hormone instead.

qs.q: An endocrinologist is evaluating a patient with a suspected pituitary adenoma. Laboratory analysis reveals a hormone composed of distinct alpha and beta glycoprotein subunits. Which hormone matches this biochemical structure?
qs.e: Thyroid-stimulating hormone is one of the glycoprotein hormones produced by the pituitary that feature alpha and beta subunits. Growth hormone is a single-chain polypeptide rather than a glycoprotein.

qs.q: A patient presents with central truncal obesity, a 'buffalo hump', purple abdominal striae, and proximal muscle wasting. Diagnostic workup reveals an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma. What is the most common overall cause of this clinical syndrome in clinical practice?
o: Ectopic ACTH production by small cell lung carcinoma
qs.e: While a pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease) is the most common endogenous cause, long-term exogenous iatrogenic corticosteroid therapy remains the most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall. Ectopic ACTH and adrenal adenomas represent other forms of endogenous excess.

qs.q: A child presents with excessive linear growth due to a growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma before epiphyseal closure. What is the clinical diagnosis?
qs.e: Gigantism results from an excess of Growth Hormone before epiphyseal closure in children. Acromegaly develops similarly but occurs in adults after epiphyseal closure.

qs.q: A patient presents with fasting hyperglycemia and is suspected of having a pituitary adenoma. What is the direct hormonal cause of elevated blood glucose in this specific condition?
qs.e: Pituitary adenoma causes hyperglycemia due to excess growth hormone secretion. Lack of cortisol would instead cause hypoglycemia as seen in Addison's disease.

qs.q: A patient experiences a sudden severe headache, bitemporal hemianopia, and acute hypopituitarism. MRI reveals hemorrhage into a pituitary adenoma. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Pituitary apoplexy is an acute complication of a pituitary adenoma, characterized by hemorrhage or infarction within the tumor. It presents with sudden severe headache, visual disturbances (bitemporal hemianopia), ophthalmoplegia, and acute hypopituitarism, often presenting with adrenal insufficiency.

qs.q: Which of the following hormone levels would be expected in a patient with Cushing's disease (pituitary adenoma)?
qs.e: Cushing's disease is caused by a pituitary adenoma secreting excess ACTH. This excess ACTH stimulates the adrenal glands to produce excessive cortisol. Therefore, both ACTH and cortisol levels are high.

es.q: A 45-year-old male presents with hypercalcemia and elevated parathyroid hormone levels. He also has a history of islet cell tumors of the pancreas and a pituitary adenoma. This constellation of findings is most consistent with which genetic syndrome? → MEN1
es.m: **Syndrome Identification**,- Most consistent with MEN1 (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1).,- Characterized by the '3 Ps': Parathyroid, Pancreas, Pituitary.,- Hypercalcaemia and elevated PTH indicate parathyroid involvement.,- Islet cell tumors (e.g., gastrinoma, insulinoma) indicate pancreatic involvement.,- Pituitary adenoma (often prolactinoma) completes the triad.,- Caused by mutation in MEN1 gene on chromosome 11q13.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Pituitary adenomas are benign tumors of anterior pituitary cells that alter hormone production or compress surrounding structures. Their size and secretory profile dictate clinical presentation and management.

sections.p: Pituitary adenomas arise from monoclonal expansion of hormone‑producing cells. They are classified by size (<1 cm micro, ≥1 cm macro) and by the hormone they secrete or by being non‑functioning.
b: Most common functional adenoma: prolactinoma
GH‑secreting adenoma → acromegaly
TSH‑secreting adenoma → rare hyperthyroidism

sections.p: Normal anterior pituitary cells synthesize peptide hormones from pre‑prohormones, regulated by hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting factors and feedback loops.
b: GH: GHRH ↑ → GH ↑ → IGF‑1 from liver
PRL: Dopamine inhibits PRL release
TSH: TRH stimulates TSH; thyroid hormone provides negative feedback

sections.p: Feedback loops keep hormone levels within narrow ranges; disruption by an adenoma leads to autonomous secretion or loss of regulation.
b: Loss of dopamine inhibition → prolactinoma hypersecretion
Uncontrolled GHRH‑independent GH release → acromegaly
TSH‑secreting adenoma bypasses thyroid hormone feedback

sections.p: Genetic mutations (e.g., MEN1, GNAS) drive clonal growth. Excess hormone causes systemic effects; mass effect compresses optic chiasm and cavernous sinus.
b: MEN1 mutation → multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
GNAS activating mutation → GH‑secreting adenoma
Macroadenoma → bitemporal hemianopsia, headache, hypopituitarism

sections.p: Patients present with hormone‑related syndromes or visual field loss. Early recognition prevents irreversible organ damage and guides targeted therapy.
b: Prolactinoma: galactorrhea, infertility, amenorrhea
Acromegaly: enlarged hands/feet, hypertension, cardiomyopathy
TSH‑adenoma: tachycardia, weight loss, goiter

t.b: Is hyperprolactinemia present? Elevated >200 ng/mL confirms prolactinoma; normal level suggests non‑functioning lesion.
Is GH excess? Elevated IGF‑1 with age‑adjusted reference indicates acromegaly; normal IGF‑1 argues against GH‑secreting tumor.
What is the size and extension? Shows micro vs macroadenoma and optic chiasm compression; if unavailable, CT can detect large lesions.

sections.p: Focus on hormone profiles, imaging findings, and syndromic clues. Remember MEN1 association and that non‑functioning adenomas present mainly with mass effect.
b: Macroadenoma >1 cm → visual field testing mandatory
Prolactin >200 ng/mL usually indicates prolactinoma, not stalk effect
GH‑adenoma: IGF‑1 elevation + lack of GH suppression on oral glucose tolerance test

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of vision or visual field defects
Rapidly worsening endocrine symptoms (e.g., thyrotoxicosis, adrenal crisis)

faq.q: Why do some pituitary adenomas cause low hormone levels?
faq.a: Large non‑functioning adenomas compress normal pituitary tissue, leading to hypopituitarism.

faq.q: Can a prolactinoma be treated without surgery?
faq.a: Yes, dopamine agonists normalize prolactin and shrink the tumor in most cases.

faq.q: What is the link between pituitary adenoma and MEN1?
faq.a: MEN1 gene mutations predispose to multiple endocrine tumors, including prolactin‑, GH‑, and TSH‑secreting adenomas.
